context: Given an integer n ≥ 2, split it into a sum of at least two positive integers. With the sum fixed at n, maximize the product of the parts.

The optimal greedy strategy takes as many factors of 3 as possible. Instead of cutting one part at a time in a loop, the code uses floor division a = n // 3 and remainder b = n % 3 to obtain the number a of length-3 parts and the remainder b directly.
description: The figure divides a bar of total length n into length-3 segments (a in all) and a segment labeled “remainder b.” Below it is the identity n = 3 × a + b, where a = n // 3, b = n % 3, and the only possible remainders are 0, 1, and 2. Placing “remainder b” on the left illustrates the decomposition symbolically. It gives no specific value for n or b and specifies no left-to-right cutting order. Ellipses between the blue length-3 segments stand for additional segments of the same length.

The following table supplements the figure with details from the text and code. The figure does not show the outcomes of these five cases. For n = 2 and n = 3, the requirement of at least two parts rules out leaving n whole.

When n ≥ 4 and b = 1, a ≥ 1, so at least one 3 is available to regroup with the remaining 1. Replace these two parts with 2 + 2. Their total length stays 4, and their product rises from 3 to 4. The number of factors of 3 drops from a to a−1, giving 3^(a−1) × 2 × 2.

frames.explanation: The “remainder b” in the figure only illustrates division with remainder. If b = 0, there is no leftover part. If b = 2, keep it as a factor. If b = 1, regroup as shown in the table. Never include 0 as a factor of the split.
frames.title: Compute the maximum product directly by case from quotient a and remainder b

summary: Use integer division and remainder to write n as 3×a+b, then adjust the split according to the remainder. Handle n=2 and n=3 separately to ensure that there are at least two parts.
